samples: This program defines a tree representation of arithmetic expressions (decimal numbers, addition, multiplication and negation), with one function that computes an expression's value and another that prints it in infix form with parentheses around every operation. Its `main` builds one small hardcoded expression and prints it alongside its result, so it works as a demo or a reusable evaluator/printer module, not a tool that reads or parses expressions from input. It is pure apart from console output, and it has no subtraction or division and no way to turn text into a tree.

This program defines a tree for arithmetic expressions (numbers, addition, multiplication and negation over decimals), with one function that computes an expression's value and another that prints it in fully parenthesized infix form. Its main function builds one hard-coded example tree and prints that expression next to its result on the console, so it works as a small demonstration rather than a tool that reads or parses your own input. It needs only console access, has no other side effects, and would suit you as a reference for recursive tree evaluation, but not if you need to evaluate expressions typed in by users.

This program defines a tree representation of arithmetic expressions (decimal numbers, addition, multiplication and negation), with one function that computes an expression's value and another that prints it in fully parenthesized infix form. Its main entry point builds one hardcoded example tree and prints it next to its result, needing only console output and no other permissions. It is a small, pure, self-contained demonstration of recursive tree handling rather than a tool that reads or parses user input, so it is useful as a building block or example, not as a calculator.

This program defines a tree representation of arithmetic expressions (decimal numbers, addition, multiplication and negation), with one function that computes an expression's value and another that prints it in infix form with parentheses around every operation. Its main entry point builds one fixed sample expression and prints it alongside its result, so it is a small demonstration of recursive evaluation and rendering rather than a tool that reads or parses user input. It is pure apart from console output and has no failure paths, so it is safe to run, but you would need to construct expression trees in code to use it for anything else.

This module defines a tree representation of arithmetic expressions (decimal numbers, addition, multiplication and negation), with one function that computes an expression's value and another that prints it in fully parenthesized infix form. Its `main` function builds a small sample expression and prints it alongside its result, so running it only writes one line to the console and touches nothing else. It is a self-contained demonstration of recursive evaluation and rendering, useful as a starting point or example, but it has no parsing of text input and supports only these four operations.
